name: Ford Model T
designer: Childe Harold Wills, Joseph A. Galamb and Eugene Farkas
assembly: Detroit, Michigan, United States (Piquette Avenue Plant, 1908–1910)

length.sourceNote: 134 in, converted at 25.4 mm/in per the infobox's own {{convert}} template. No qualifier is given, unlike width and height below.

wheelbase.sourceNote: 100 in, converted at 25.4 mm/in. Constant across the whole 1908–1927 run and every body style.

kerbWeight.sourceNote: The infobox publishes a single range for the whole car, 1,200–1,650 lb, converted at 0.45359237 kg/lb to 544.3–748.4 kg. It is not attributed to a specific body style or year, so the lighter bound is recorded here per the project convention for a published range (record the lower bound, state the full range here) — this is the published floor, not a measurement of any one trim.

trims.name: Runabout
trims.transmission: Planetary gear, two forward speeds plus reverse — contemporary sources called it a "three-speed", counting reverse as a gear

displacement.sourceNote: 177 cu in, converted at 16.387064 cc/cu in; the infobox's own {{convert}} template rounds this to 2.9 L. One engine specification for the entire 1908–1927 run — Ford's stated philosophy was to keep the car itself unchanged.

power.sourceNote: 20 hp (mechanical horsepower), converted at 1 hp = 0.745699872 kW. The same figure is given for the whole production run; no per-year or per-body-style output is published.

topSpeed.sourceNote: 42 mph, converted at 1.609344 km/mph. No 0-100 km/h figure is recorded because the car's stated top speed never reaches 100 km/h — omission, not a gap.

fuelEconomy.sourceNote: Ford's published range was 13-21 mpg (US), quoted for the engine rather than for a body style. Recorded as the low end in the unit stored — 21 mpg = 11.20 L/100 km, converted at 235.215 L-mi/100km-gal — with the full range stated here. The other end of the range is 18.09 L/100 km.

mass.sourceNote: The infobox's model-wide 1,200–1,650 lb range, lower bound, converted at 0.45359237 kg/lb. Not attributed to this body style specifically — the two-seat Runabout was almost certainly toward the light end, but the source does not say so.

width.sourceNote: Explicitly qualified in the infobox as "(1912 roadster)" — the only body style and year Wikipedia gives a width for, which is why it is recorded on this trim rather than at generation level.

height.sourceNote: Also qualified "(1912 roadster)" in the infobox, alongside the width above.

frontalArea.sourceNote: Derived, not published: the site's standing approximation of 0.85 x width x height, using the 1912 roadster's own sourced width and height (1,676 x 1,860 mm). No drag coefficient or measured frontal area exists for the Model T to check this estimate against — it predates the era when Wikipedia's automobile drag-coefficient list has data.

prices.sourceNote: Launch-year price, from the article's production/price table.
The cheapest year of the whole run — a 68% nominal price fall from 1909, which the article attributes to the 1913 moving assembly line and the scale it enabled.
Final full model year; the price table notes production ended before mid-1927 to allow retooling for the Model A.

displacement.sourceNote: 177 cu in, converted at 16.387064 cc/cu in; the infobox's own {{convert}} template rounds this to 2.9 L. One engine specification for the entire 1908–1927 run.

power.sourceNote: 20 hp (mechanical horsepower), converted at 1 hp = 0.745699872 kW. The same figure is given for the whole production run.

topSpeed.sourceNote: 42 mph, converted at 1.609344 km/mph. No 0-100 km/h figure is recorded because the car's top speed never reaches 100 km/h.

fuelEconomy.sourceNote: Ford's published range was 13-21 mpg (US), quoted for the engine rather than for a body style. Recorded as the low end in the unit stored — 21 mpg = 11.20 L/100 km, converted at 235.215 L-mi/100km-gal — with the full range stated here. The other end of the range is 18.09 L/100 km.

prices.sourceNote: Noted in the price table against the same year's $825 Runabout.
Noted in the price table against the same year's $260 Runabout — a 66% nominal fall from 1909.

hero.alt: A 1925 Ford Model T Touring car in dark green, photographed from the front three-quarter angle with its canvas top raised, brass-trimmed radiator shell and wood-spoke wheels on balloon tyres
hero.caption: A 1925 Touring car — by this point riding on the balloon tyres and split rims that arrived as options in the Model T's last two years.

gallery.caption: Ford's own full-page advertisement for the very first Model T, from the October 1, 1908 issue of Life magazine — the car as it looked the week production began.

gallery.alt: Close-up of the Model T's three floor pedals, labelled left to right as clutch, reverse and brake
gallery.caption: The whole control layout in one photograph: left pedal for the planetary clutch, centre for reverse, right for the transmission brake — there were no brakes on the wheels at all.

gallery.alt: Black-and-white photograph of Ford's 1913 moving assembly line, with rows of Model T chassis under construction
gallery.caption: The 1913 Highland Park moving assembly line — the innovation that did more to define the Model T's history than any single body style did.
